speechtext:
Mr. Kendall does not say the statement is true, but that Daivey Wais-

Customs Inquiry-Mr. Donaghy
berg said this to him. I do not for a moment suppose that Waisberg would feel 5 p.m. himself under any obligation to disclose to Kendall anything except his own version of what would suit his interest, and I hope my hon. friend is not more credulous than I am in regard to the workings of smugglers of his type. I proceed with the letter:
The following are some of the questions and answers:
This was a smart boy, and when the conversation was over he apparently wrote down the questions and answers from memory:
Q. Are you aware of the penalty you are liable to?
A. Yes, but you are white, you would not let it out.
Q. There has been a lot of this going on? It seems to me -there is a gang working, and you are most likely one of them?
A. No, I am working myself.
Q. You have in this trunk some valuable merchandise what is it worth?

Q. If I would accept your bribe I would be liable to imprisonment.
A. Here, take this $50, I have it all counted ready, and nobody will be the wiser. Barrie is the easiest place because you are alone in examining.
Q. Why did you not go to Mr. Young?
A. I knew he would not let it through. You need the money, he does not. It would be no use asking him.
Q. Do you think I have no conscience, and hold my oath of office as a joke?
A. Oaths are nothing. You need the money. Here it is. It is easy for you and easy for me. You are white, and can be well off in a few months. Remember this is a steady thing.
The letter then proceeds:
I seized the trunk, and had it locked in the bond room after resealing it. When I told Waisberg that I was not here all the time, but was out relieving sometimes, he replied that it would be easy for me to go away if I wished, or he would wait until I came back to Barrie.
I have the honour to be, Sir,
Your obedient servant,
C. R. Kendall, Customs Clerk-Examiner.
I want to emphasize this point. These two original communications were received by the Deputy Minister of Customs and apparently later brought to the attention of the Hon. Jacques Bureau. I said that Mr. W. A. Boys, K.C., M.P., appeared at the Customs office and saw Collector young. The following letter was then written by Mr. Boys to the deputy minister at Ottawa, under date of October 25, 1922:
R. R. Farrow, Esq.,
Commissioner of Customs,
Ottawa.
My Dear Mr. Farrow :
Re D. Waisberg
I would like to see you herein. Kindly delay proceedings-
(Mr. Donaghy.]
This reminds me of another case of which we have heard. Shall we make the welkin ring with condemnation of that phrase? Perhaps not now.
Kindly delay proceedings until Friday morning, the 27th, when I will be in Ottawa, and I will call and see you at 10.30.
Sincerely,
W. A. Boys.
P.S.-I presume you are familiar with the matter, if not, I think Mr. Taylor is.
Now we will see what happened next, and you will have to read between the lines of t'he next letter. On November 7, 1922, the Hon. Jacques Bureau, Minister of Customs, wrote the following letter to Mr. Boys:
Re Waisberg
W. A. Boys, Esquire, M.P.,
Barrie.
My Dear Boys,-After your visit to my office with reference to the above, I sent for the file and went through it very carefully. I presume that Mr. Waisberg did not represent to you the facts as they were, so that you might judge for yourself.
I am sending you a copy of part of the file which will explain itself.
If he sent for the file he 'would read these two letters from C. Kendall:
Under the circumstances I do not think I would be justified in exercising any special leniency towards Mr. Waisberg.
That is the considered opinion of the minster, and we will see later on if the minister was persuaded:
You will see by tlhis (part of the file which I enclose herewith that the case is more serious than you thought or than you represented it to me. If Mr. Waisberg has been the man you represented him to be, I am afraid he is not now of the same calibre and that it will be dangerous to in any way condone or show leniency before further action ia taken.
I will wait till I hear from you.
Yours very truly,
Minister of Customs and Excise.
Then on November 13, Mr. Boys wrote the Hon. Mr. Bureau as follows:
Hon. Jacques Bureau,
House of Commons,
Ottawa.
My Dear Mr. Bureau,-I have to be in Ottawa on Friday and will call and see you re Waisberg, so kindly let the matter stand .till then.
Sincerely yours,
W. A. Boys.
I believe my hon. friend wants to be fair, so why does he pass over the letter which I wrote before that

I will be very glad to read it; it would be only fair to read all the letters.

Customs Inquiry-Mr. Donaghy
I do not want you to do that but I would like this previous letter to be put in.
I will be very glad to read this letter; it is undated.
It is not undated.

Mr. Bell asked the question :
Tiie date is what?
Mr. Oalder, K.C.:	It is undated, but it follows
immediately upon the letter dated November 27th, and it precedes the letter dated November 13th.
Mr. Bell: I am trying to get the year.
Mr. Caider, K.C.:	1922.
The letter is not dated, but I will read it: Re Waisberg Hon. Jacques Bureau,
House o-f Commons,
Ottawa.
Dear Mr. Bureau,-I have just received your letter and naturally regret that you feel disinclined to adopt the suggestion you made during our interview. I note you -think the case more serious -than presented by me. I really do not think this conclusion is justified.
As far as I know, I told you Waisberg had attempted to bribe a customs officer and I intimated he had been persistent, and I also told you he had pulled out $50 in money and offered it.
I d d say I was of the opinion he was not making it a business and his crude effort in my opinion warrants that conclusion.
Do not be too dramatic.

Mr. Speaker, the simplicity of mind displayed in this letter is really amusing:
Aftr all, the offence of'which Waisberg was guilty
was exactly as I stated.
As you know, I did not ask that he should go scot-free and I felt now, having to pay double duty and sales tax, he is being severely penalized, and unless you think he is a confirmed smuggler or one of a gang, I am still of the opinion that for this, his first offence, the penalty suggested is very severe.
I reported the result of my trip to him and to his wife, and it will certainly come as a serious blow if oriminal proceedings are now taken, and I trust, upon further consideration, you will see your way clear to carry out the arrangement made when I was with you.
Oh, oh.
Would the hon. member please explain the joke?
Order.
I did not catch my hon. friend's remark.
I asked if the hen. member would be pleased to explain the joke.

I have a very high
opinion of the perspicacity of the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) when he wants to see the point.
I do not think you should lay too much stress upon the question and answer portion of the interview. No stenographer was present, and it as purely from memory.
It is true, it seems very impressive, but after all it ift a case of attempted bribery and I definitely presented fit as such, and I would be sorry to -have you think I did not represent it according to the facts.
In view of the incident alleged and an view of Mr. Young's letter requesting you to deal leniently, and in view of the fact that it is his first offence, 1 think justice will be done by carrying out the arrangement made, and if you do not feel free to so dispose of it, I would be glad if you would let it stand until I again see you.
I think I will be in Ottawa next week on other business and at the very worst, will be there on the 27th or 28th, at which time I am to interview the Acting Minister of Railways, and in the meantime the only person suffering is Waisberg, for his goods are under seizure.
Yours sincerely,
W. A. Boys.

Tell us what
happened to Waisberg.
Ask your own whip.

I will now proceed with
the reading of a letter that I was requested to read. On November 1.3th Mr. Boys wrote to Mr. Bureau as follows:
My dear Mr. Bureau,
I have to be in Ottawa on Friday and will call and se you re Waisberg so kindly let the matter stand till then.
On December 13th Mr. Boys again wrote Mr. Bureau as follows:
Hon. Jacques Bureau,
Minister of Customs,
Ottawa.
Dear Mr. Bureau,
Re Waisberg
I have had no word herein as yet, and unfortunately the silk in question is still being held. I saw Mr. Young, customs officer, and he told me he had received no word. I would be excedingly obliged if you would give the necessary instructions to the local officer to release the silk on receipt of the amount payable.
Sincerely yours,
W. A. Boys.
The Hon. Jacques Bureau was eventually pursuaded and he did order the release of the silk.
On payment of how much?

Wait a moment until
I find the amount.
The amount was $813.60.
Now I have it here. This trunk of silk was returned to Waisberg on the order of the Hon. Jacques Bureau-
Two years afterwards.

Ye3, two years afterwards on payment of $813.60. I am now going

Customs Inquiry-Mr. Donaghy
to read to you the evidence of Mr. Blair, departmental solicitor and assistant to the deputy, as to how that came about. Mr. Blair's evidence is set out at page 1666 of the evidence and will be found very interesting reading. I quote as follows:
Q. Mr. Blair, at that moment, you knew this attempt at bribery could be proven?
A. Yes. I would like to explain with regard to that. You will see the date-
Q. Yes, 7/3/24.
A. Away in the fa!! of 1924. The matter had stood all that time. I know from conversations with the deputy minister concerning it, that he was very anxious Waisberg should be prosecuted on both charges, and that the goods should bo forfeited, and there is no question but that is what should have been done. It dragged along, as you will see. The goods were lying there, and depreciating, and he finally called me into his office, and said "You had better prepare a report."
This is one of those "instructed" reports which members of the committee have severely condemned. Instead of departmental officers being allowed to prepare their own reports, they are instructed from those higher up as to what to put into their recommendations. That is what happened in this Waisberg case I continue to quote:
Q. Who told you that?
A. The commissioner. He said "Because it is the intention of the minister to release these goods upon payment of double duty," according to a promise he had given Mr. Boys. I should never have signed that. You will see that is a carbon copy. That is not my recommendation.
That is the report as to release on payment of double duty. I continue quoting:
Q. But the recommendation was prepared by you at Mr. Farrow's request?
A. His instructions.
Q. But Mr. Farrow, at that time, was very strongly disinclined to abandon prosecution?
A. Yes, that was the cause of all the delay.
Here were these poor subordinate officers in the department trying to get a prosecution for bribery under the Criminal Code against this man and they could not get it, they were held back.
That is not a fair statement.

I will read the quotation again, and the hon. gentleman will judge if it is not a fair statement:
Q. But Mr. Farrow at that time was very strongly disinclined t-o abandon prosecution?
A. Yes, tiiat was the cause of all the delay.
I hope I have satisfied the hon. gentleman.

The hon. gentleman will admit the evidence shows there was not the slightest effort in any way to settle the attempt at bribery?
Soma hon MEMRERS: Order.
I suppose hon. gentlemen want to be fair?
No, they do not.

The whole circumstance
will have to speak for itself. In this case there was no prosecution for bribery or no prosecution for smuggling or attempted smuggling as there should have been. All that was done was that the Minister of Customs at the request of, and as the result of an agreement made with, Mr. Boys, prevented the law from being carried into effect as it should have been and in the most flagrant case that was brought before the whole committee-this most outstanding case of criminality, of an attempt to take advantage of a poor boy with sickness in his family-punishment was thwarted. Under these circumstances the facts will have to speak for themselves; I make no comment upon them.
What about Moser?
Moses is all right.

I continue quoting from
Mr. Blair's evidence:
Q. And 'it. was against his recommendation, and his desire to prosecute, (that the goods were released on payment of double duty and sales tax?
A. Yes. He was very anxious for the man to be prosecuted from the start.
And he was thwarted in trying to discharge his duty.
Have you any condemnation for the minister?

I am now going to deal
with another very interesting case.
Will you permit me one question?
Undoubtedly.

I do not want to interrupt my hon. friend 'but if he is through with the Waisberg case I should like to ask him this question:	Does he suggest to the House
that there was anything in my conduct which warranted the reporting of the evidence to the House, and if so why he did not vote in favour of it in the committee?

In order to answer that question, I have to give the reasons why we brought in a report without condemning members of parliament. If the hon. member wants that explanation I am prepared to give it now.

My hon. friend knows that I appeared before the committee without any summons and made my statement. I invited

Customs Inquiry-Mr. Donaghy
the committee-and he was present at the time-to make any charge they thought fit against me and to report it to the House if they saw fit, and they did not do so.
The hon. member has not answered my question as to what he desired me to do, and I am going to exercise my own discretion in the matter now.
I will invite the hon. member to go as far as he likes.

I propose to tell this House why, in that report, we omitted to bring in any condemnation of members of parliament or to mention their names. Personally I felt that in the interests of this country a report should be brought in that would have the support of both sides of the House in reference to all its recommendations for improving conditions in this country. 1 felt that the people were more interested in the welfare of the country and the revenue of this country than they were in a discussion in that committee of party politics and personal differences.
When did the hon. member change his mind?

The remark of the hon. member discloses amazing ignorance. I fancy he has not read the report. The report is as I have stated and I have not changed my miind; but I had in view the bringing in of a unanimous report in the interest of the country and to satisfy the demands of the House; and the evidence having been reported to the House, it was then open to discuss, in connection with that evidence, any matter reflecting upon ministers, members, or whoever it might be. I have not made any charge against the hon. member, as he well knows. I have refrained from doing so, and I have taken this position: I have stated the facts, and if these facts do not carry conviction it is not my fault. It is my duty to give the facts. These facts and circumstances speak for themselves.
Now I turn to the case of Moses Aziz, which I am sure will bring smiles of joy to the countenances of my hon. friends opposite. We find that Moses Aziz, of the province of New Brunswick, was charged with ' importing into Canada and having in his possession some kegs of liquor. He was convicted on the 18tih August last. This all occurred before the new Minister of Customs had any idea that he was ever going to be Minister of Customs. Some question was raised last night as to whether or not the charge laid against Moses Aziz was as
severe a charge as should have been laid. I do know that, the present Minister of Customs had nothing to do with it and is not responsible, for it. On the 29th of August. 1925, Mr. Gallagher, the solicitor in charge of the Remission branch which deals with clemency and pardon for offences, wrote a letter to the Customs department regarding the Moses Aziz case. I point out to hon. members that that was in August, prior to the new Minister of Customs having been sworn in or appointed. The letter is from M. F. Gallagher, Chief of the Remission branch. It does not say to what officer it is addressed, but presumably it is to some official in the Customs department. The letter reads:
Dear Sir.-Representations have been made to the hon. the Minister of Justice, by the Premier of New Brunswick - on the case of Moses A. M. Aziz, convicted at Bathurst on August 18, of illegal possession of illicitly imported liquor. A fine of $150 was imposed, together with a jail sentence of three months, and the fine has been paid. The Premier of New Brunswick suggests that the imprisonment be suspended-
I do not know whether or not that has been called to the attention of hon. members.
It was read last night.

The suggestion originated with the Premier of New Brunswick, and under our constitution the administration and enforcement of laws of a criminal character are in the hands of provincial governments. The letter proceeds:
The Premier of New Brunswick suggests that the imprisonment be suspended, as the offender is a mamied man, in business for himself, and the term of imprisonment will occasion him much hardship.
From my experience as a lawyer I can safely say that that plea is very frequently advanced as a ground for exercising clemency, namely, the hardship the sentence will impose upon a man's family. It has often been advanced in cases of liquor conviction, and often acceded to. The letter proceeds.
Moreover, it is stated that Aziz was not aware that the mere possession of smuggled liquor was in itself an offence, and further that the possession dated long before the act was amended.
As this man is not imprisoned, the Minister of Justice cannot order has release; it therefore, is a matter for your department to decide whether or not the magistrate should be asked to issue a warrant of commitment.
Yours truly,
M. F. Gallagher.
The suggestion came from Mr. Gallagher that it was a matter for the Department of Customs to decide.

Read the remainder of
the letter.
4S9S

Customs Inquiry-Mr. Donaghy
I have read it all. The only thing I did not read was the words, "Chief of Remission branch" below the signature. I could not go any further down, much as I would like to oblige my hon. friend.

The letter I refer to
was the one from the Premier of New Brunswick.

I was not reading that.
If my hon. friend wants me to read two letters at the same time he will be sadly disappointed. At the time that letter was written the new Minister of Customs had not been appointed. He is not responsible for that letter in any shape or form and he is not responsible for the recommendation of the Premier of New Brunswick, nor is he responsible for the suggestion made by Mr. Gallagher, the chief of the Remission branch. He does not come into the scene until away on in September; he was sworn in on the fifth of that month. He did not assume the active discharge of the duties of his office until the end of October. As the House will remember, many ministers were absent from Ottawa during those two months. The minister, however, attended a cabinet meeting about the 21st September, 1925, a long time after this man had been convicted. He went from that cabinet meeting to his office in the Customs department and he was there, for a very short time. The accumulation of months of work and files was on his desk, neglected. Those of us who have had to do with large offices will appreciate what that means. During the short time he was there and knowing that he would be staying there only a few hours, he dealt with what matters he could as presented to him by the officials under him, his deputy and others. The Aziz file was presented and it was explained to him that this man had been convicted a month ago; that he had not been imprisoned, and that apparently the Premier of New Brunswick had asked that the case be held up in the meantime.
What did the new Minister of Customs decide then? If this man was convicted over a month ago and some steps had been taken to hold up his imprisonment in the meantime at the request of the Premier of New Brunswick, any man would feel satisfied that that step must have been taken legally. We know how these things are handled in Ontario. I know how they are handled in British Columbia. When a man is convicted and he stands in the dock and sentence is imposed for three months' imprisonment, one officer hangs on to one arm and another on to the other and

he is taken down below to the cells. If the next day you find him on the street you would never suspect that he had escaped. You would suppose, as any lawyer would suppose, that his solicitor had taken the necessary legal proceedings either by way of appeal and getting the man out on bail pending appeal, or in some other manner. Had I gone into the office of the Minister of Customs in the middle of September last and been informed by officials there in a hurried interview that this man had been convicted a month ago and that his imprisonment had been held up in the meantime, I say frankly as a lawyer that I would assume, without further question, that the usual procedure had been gone through to have that man released pending appeal or whatever proceedings had been taken, or pending certiorari proceedings which might also be taken. There were two ways in which he might have been out. The minister told us that while this was called to his attention he did not take the time to read the letter which had been written to the Hon. Jacques Bureau by Mr. Robiohaud. He said: "I gave this matter what consideration I could. I said: If representations are being made and there are some circumstances connected with the case, my order is to let them stand as they are until they can be investigated." It was an exercise of judgment.
The minister appeared before the committee. He told us: "I do not want to shield myself in any manner, shape or form. I want to tell you the worst about myself in connection with this case." That statement carried to me at least an air of conviction, of sincerity, of proof of his high sense of honour. The sting in the whole thing is contained in the letter which Mr. Robichaud wrote. We cannot hold anybody responsible for writing a letter like that other than the man who writes it. Nobody with any sense of public honour would attempt to justify the expressions used by Mr. Robichaud in that letter and I am not going to attempt to justify them. My selfrespect will not permit it. The sting, I say, is in that letter and it is contained in these words in the letter which Robichaud wrote to Mr. Bureau, not to Mr. Boivin:
Mr. Aziz is of the highest help for us during this campaign, and we cannot do without his services.
That is the sting. I think there is another letter with a similar sting. Mr. Speaker, I ask you and I ask parliament as the highest court in this country, if it can, in the fairness which parliament will exercise, condemn the new Minister of Customs because an expression of that kind was contained in a

Customs Inquiry-Mr. Donaghy
letter written by a gentleman who, to speak charitably, was most indiscreet, and addressed to the Hon. Jacques Bureau. Parliament, I say, will be fair in exercising its judicial function as the highest court in the land. As a result of that hurried consideration which the minister gave to the Aziz case the deputy minister or Mr. Wilson, the chief preventive officer, sent a telegram to the lawyer acting for the department in New Brunswick asking him to hold the case up in the meantime.
The new Minister of Customs did not return to take over his duties until the end of October, and I now proceed to inquire: What did he do in regard to this case when he got it under his hand? Let me read from page 1324 of the inquiry, and I crave the careful attention of members while I read the judgment of the minister. The new Minister of Customs writes this letter:
Ottawa, November 18, 1925. Mr. J. G. Robichaud, M.P.,
Shippigan, N.B.
Dear Sir:-
I have before me a memorandum concerning the case of Mr. Moses Aziz, who was condemned by the court to a fine of $150 and to three months' imprisonment for having had liquor in his possession.
The fine of $150 was paid, but the execution of the warrant of commitment was temporarily suspended.
I have examined the case with care, and I can find no reason for which the imposed sentence should not be executed.
That is the judgment of the minister when he had time to bring his mind to bear upon
the case.
I have examined the case with care, and I can find no reason for which the imposed sentence should not be executed, but I will keep the matter in suspense until I get a repfly from you, in the event of your having other representations to make to me.
The officers of the department contend that the efforts made to prevent smuggling of liquors will be much lessened df this man is let go without further punishment.
That is the judgment of the minister, exercising a high sense of duty in the performance of his office.
Oh, oh.

Hon. gentlemen laugh
at that, but I fail to see the reason. Now what happened following that? Remember, that was November 18 and parliament was summoned for December 10. It is not necessary for me to picture to the House with what matters members of the cabinet were concerned immediately succeeding that date, nor is it necessary for me to tell you what crisis faced the government. It was well known in the country at the time and I have no doubt that frequent, probably daily meetings of the cabinet were being held. Apart from
that I need hardly say that hundreds of other cases calling for decision by the minister awaited consideration in the office of the Department of Customs. Can parliament regard this Moses Aziz case as the only matter that was before the Minister of Customs at that time? It is suggested that he should have disposed of it promptly; he should have brought Mr. Robichaud here the next day if possible after pronouncing that judgment. But let us look at the circumstances as they existed at the time. The Aziz case did not fill the whole picture in the countiy's eye, for more serious matters demanded the attention of the government. Parliament, although summoned for December 10, did not meet until January 7, and in the interval we can readily conceive what matters the members of the cabinet were called upon to consider. And when the House did meet on January 7, according to hon. gentlemen opposite, the Minister of Customs should have sent immediately for Mr. Robichaud, who had come up from New Brunswick. Why, it is asked, did not the Minister of Customs get into touch with Mr. Robichaud immediately and deal with the case? Have we, Mr. Speaker, no just sense of proportion regarding the importance of matters of public concern? When parliament met on January 7 there were other and graver and more vital interests occupying the attention of ministers, as they had occupied their attention for weeks. We all know the debate which followed for a month, and the uncertainty as to whether this government would remain in power or be voted out any day of the week. We know with what unremitting attendance members of the House were obliged to be here. They dared not leave the building, and pairs for most of the time were refused. When every member was in attendance day and night in this chamber, do hon. gentlemen insist that the Minister of Customs could have disposed of the Aziz case more expeditiously than he did? Let us be reasonable in these things. Let us as the high court of, parliament sitting in judgment in this case be fair in the treatment we mete out to the minister against whom this oharge is made. Shall we, for any political advantage, sitting here as the highest court in the land commit an injustice on a British subject? The eyes of all Canada are on parliament to-day. The people are wondering what the House will do with the Customs report, a report which has met with the universal approval of the business element of Canada. The business men of this country are wondering whether we are going to proceed with business and carry out the
Privilege-Mr. Forke

recommendations of the report or sit back in this House and play politics and try to " get " one another.
A great deal of fuss has been made about the Aziz case. Now, in the province of Ontario last year 252 remissions of sentence were granted bootleggers and violators of the Ontario Temperance Act. I am not criticising that. These applications for clemency had no doubt been supported by persons influential in the community. Offenders generally call upon the local member to help them out when their familes are in distress and when they want to get out of gaol. These things are not new in Canada, but the Moses Aziz case is now brought out and an attempt is made to create a great political issue upon it. Smuggling has been going on for years; it has been going on under the administrations of both parties. The condition in which we found the administration of the customs, in the investigation we made, was the result of years of accumulated neglect. It is not a sudden growth, as everyone knows. Had time permitted, and had the Liberal members of the committee so desired, we might have made efforts to delve back into the administration of the Customs department during the past ten years, and I have no doubt some things could have been unearthed. For my part, these tactics do not appeal to me. If the administration of the Customs department under the Liberal party had not been properly carried out it would, to my mind, be no excuse to say, "Neither was it properly carried out under the Conservative government." I do not want to take that stand. No attempt was made to go back into the Conservative regime.
The press of the country has been free in its criticism of the display made by the two political parties during the present session. There is a strong suspicion in the mind of the public that political parties are wearing a mask of hypocrisy, and that behind many of these attacks and manoeuvres there is simply the design to play the game of beating the other side.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

speechtext:
I know it will be pleasant to hon. gentlemen opposite if I do not dwell too long upon the various questions that arose during the customs inquiry which lasted some four and a half months. When the Minister of Customs and Excise (Mr. Boivin) spoke at Sherbrooke on March 21 last and said that this inquiry would cost the country something like a half a million dollars, with no good results, it was the opinion of the members of the committee that the hon. minister had erred somewhat. He admitted that yesterday, and for his admission we are grateful. He said yesterday, Mr. Speaker, that politics had crept into the inquiry during the first few weeks. If politics were brought in I ask who was responsible? The first clash that came in the committee was when we asked on March 3 that the Duncan report be placed in evidence, and that Inspector Duncan himself be called into the witness box -to testify as to the accuracy of that report. Tiie first division in the committee occurred then, and had it not been for the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett), the hon. member for West Hamilton (Mr. Bell), the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Kennedy) and myself voting together to have the Duncan report placed in evidence, thus securing a majority, that report would not have been produced. Listening to the arguments of the hon. member for North Vancouver this afternoon one would imagine his party were entitled to all the credit for conducting this inquiry because forsooth they had produced the Duncan report. Do hon. members of this House realize that on April 21 we made a motion to have the Duncan report included in the evidence? The chairman of the committee then invoked, as he had a right to do, a rule which had not been invoked during a period of six or eight weeks. He asked that notice of motion be given and that the question be deferred for decision until the following Tuesday. It was not until the hon. member for Peace River

supported our motion that the supporters of the government yielded to our wishes.
Now, Sir, I turn to other phases of the question Certain rumours are afloat, and in view of that fact I am not surprised at the question that was directed to me before I had even begun my speech. I can foresee by the rumours to-day that if the questions of conscription, the war with Turkey, and all the other familiar election cries of the past cannot be resorted to, one issue that will be raised at the next election will be that this committee focussed its searchlight only upon the port of Montreal in the province of Quebec. Let me say that if the committee focussed its searchlight upon the port of Montreal there are very many reasons for that First of all, Montreal is the largest port in this Dominion. In the next place it is the second largest port on the North American continent. Furthermore, Montreal is the fifth largest city on the continent; it is the metropolis of the Dominion, it is the chief manufacturing centre, and owing to its geographical position it serves approximately seventy-five per cent of the country's population.

speechtext:
I am convinced, although
I am not boasting about it, that my remarks this evening will make much more impression on my friends on this side than if the hon. member had himself spoken.
With reference to the conditions in the port of Montreal and the province of Quebec since 1922, the attention of the commercial interests of the countiy was focussed upon that section. On the 13th of January, 1922, the ex-Mmister of Customs caused the detachment of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police stationed at Lacolle to be removed from there, thus making easy the way of the transgressor in defrauding the public revenue. On the 25th of March, 1922, the same Minister had the Royal Canadian Mounted Police detachment removed from Philipsburg, Quebec, thereby opening the highway crossing the international boundary, providing an opportunity for the smuggler to import contraband goods into this country. On the 6th of May,' 1924, the same Minister of Customs instructed the Royal Canadian Mounted Police force in Montreal to do nothing but report to Bisaillon. On the 24th of October, 1924, the same gentleman, occupying the position of Minister of Customs and Excise, removed all authority as customs and excise officers from the Royal Canadian Mounted

Customs Inquiry-Mr. Doucet
Police force at Montreal. Do you know, Sir, that the removal of Chief Inspector Busby from his inspectorship of the division of Montreal and the substitution of an inefficient and incapable successor, made the way much easier for wholesale corruption of the public service? Notorious cases arose in this district. Let me cite the Keith-Vaughan-Harrison case, referred to by my hon. friend from Vancouver North (Mr. Donaghy) this afternoon; the famous S. S. "Borden" drug case, the famous barge "Tremblay" case, and again the Denise Larde silk smuggling case into the port of Quebec. There were very many cases of this kind, and the commercial interests of the Dominion were affected. They centralized on the Commercial Protective Association, and they asked that special men be sent to Montreal to investigate. And let me say that the steps taken by the Finance department in sending men to inspect the port of Montreal, and the information gathered thereby, were the basis upon which this inquiry was conducted. The fact, again, that the counsel chosen for the committee had intimate knowledge of the way smugglers were carrying on their nefarious traffic in this section gave him firsthand knowledge as to how to proceed with the inquiry. That he was a clever gentleman and that his work was done in an efficient manner no one will deny, and that he was likewise appointed by this government is admitted by all. Then I ask, Mr. Speaker, how is it that the inquiry was focussed at first on Montreal, to the detriment of that city? Respectable citizens of Montreal and respectable citizens of the whole province of Quebec have welcomed this inquiry, and the facts revealed by it will be the means of cleaning out the smuggling gang operating in that section, will give a fair chance to the legitimate business interests of the province to conduct business, and will also bring additional revenue to the treasury of this Dominion.
During the first addresses made on the charges preferred by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) on the 2nd of February last, and referred to, it is true in a very small degree, by the hon. member for Vancouver North this afternoon, the Civil Service Commission was practically accused of having made a poor selection of the Customs officers in that section. I hold no brief for the Civil Service Commission, but the revelations made by that committee were such that two of the commissioners were asked by the Prime Minister to tender their resignations.

speechtext:
I accept the explanation of the right hon. gentleman. It is satisfactory to me. It meant the same thing, and in fact it was the same thing. I hold no brief for that commission, but I want to say that the files and the evidence produced before the committee clearly show that every man who was neglectful in his duties was appointed to the force before the Civil Service Commission appointed men to the outside service. Furthermore, every promotion made by the Civil Service Commission was recommended by the department itself before the promotion went through. The inspector of the port of Montreal was recommended as 100 per cent efficient, 100 per cent capable, and by whom? By officers of the department; and if he did not get a reclassification last year, was it the fault of the department? We have in evidence, Mr. Speaker, that the deputy minister harassed the commission for six months to give this man Clerk a reclassification, and the reclassifioation would have gone through if it had not been objected to by the chairman of that commission. It is useless to try to blame the Civil Service Commission for the negligence in the customs service. Do hon. gentlemen want any further proof? You remember, Mr. Speaker, when the vote for $350,000 passed this House last session, the plea was made by the Prime Minister himself. If we refer to page 3778 of last year's Hansard, we will see that he said that it is most important that steps should be taken to protect the revenue of this country. There was a loss in revenue of possibly fifty to a hundred million dollars per year owing to the conditions that existed, and the Minister of Customs himself said, "You cannot get efficient officers by applying to the Civil Service Commission. These men must be appointed outside of that commission altogether." With what result? The records of sixty-seven special men were placed before the committee, and I am going to quote a few of them this evening for the purpose of showing that they got poorer results than they would have obtained if they had asked the commission to make the appointments.
In the fall of 1924 there were some 123 cans of alcohol seized at St. Leonard in the county of Madawaska, New Brunswick. That



Customs Inquiry-Mr. Doucet
alcohol was placed in the customs house for safe keeping. The man in charge of that warehouse left the place about thirty minutes after midnight on the 21st of December and went to a pool room where he played cards until about six o'clock in the morning. When he returned he found that the place had been broken open, the alcohol was gone and he had no excuse to offer. That is in substance the report given by the inspector of customs stationed at Woodstock, New Brunswick. The man, as would be expected, was retired; but when it came to the appointment of a special preventive officer in October last, the same man was appointed at a salary of $1,200 a year.
I come to the case of a man at Chester, Nova Scotia, a man who was fined in October 1922 for having sixteen gallons of smuggled rum in his possession. The files of the department show that he was appointed as a special preventive officer on the recommendation of the member for the constituency, and when the chief of the preventive service said: "Why, this man is a noted smuggler," this member, (Mjr. Duff), wired back, "collect" as per usual, stating: "He is a good mian."
I come to the case of three men appointed in the county of Gloucester in the month of October. One of them is eighty-four years of age.

subtopic: REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext:
I have no objection to
having questions put to me, but I wish the hon. gentleman when rising to a point of order would have something to talk on. I can give him my assurance now that I do not propose to treat him as badly as the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Donaghy) treated him this afternoon. I did not intend to use any harsh language in this connection and I do not intend to do so now.
I wish to finish my point with this observation. When the three men were appointed to the force of Gloucester in October last, the man who took them to the magistrate to have them sworn in was the famous Moses Aziz who had been convicted. On the files of the department produced before the committee there are letters to the department from officers in good standing down there who claim that Moses Aziz had been the medium through whom those three officers were reporting to the Customs department. Why, this question of going outside the Civil Service Commission to appoint preventive officers is considered in the Maritime provinces to be a huge joke. No later than three weeks ago a customs officer had to be appointed to the outport of Chartierville in the county of Compton, Quebec. Who was appointed? A man who has violated the cus-

Customs Inquiry-Mr. Doucet
toms law and has been fined therefor, a man who is a noted smuggler in that part of the country.
Need I say anything in connection with the appointment of Captain Zinck of Lunenburg?
I do not wish to say anything detrimental to him because he has passed to the great beyond, although he had not when the inquiry was being held. But when in 1924 the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) put on Hansard a question asking what salary Captain Zinck was getting, the hon. member was told that Captain Zinck did not receive any salary. Can hon. members imagine a man such as Captain Zinck working day and night surveying the liquor-laden vessels coming into the port of Lunenburg, without salary? He did not. When it was found by an inspector of the department that he had to refund over $2,600 of the moneys of this Dominion, then the department gave him a salary of $100 a month. In connection with the special preventive service, one Mr. Trask was appointed on October 1, 1925, to the position of customs preventive officer, and on the 14th of that month he made two seizures of liquors and of one schooner. That man was discharged on October 19. In fairness to the member for tlhe constituency it must be said that a Charge was made against this officer, but I would point out that the information on the files shows that an affidavit or a declaration made by a well known smuggler was taken in preference to his. And by the way, these seizures which Mr. Trask had made were abandoned and no prosecution was pursued by the department.
I come now to the appointment a!, Mahone bay on September 1, 1925, of an officer whose selection was made upon recommendation by collect telegram despatched by the representative of the constituency, the member for Lunenburg, (Mr. Duff). This officer took his instructions from the member of the riding and reported to Captain Zinck, and when questioned by the preventive service in the month of January, 1926, as to why he had done no work, he replied, "Why, gentlemen, in September and October I was occupied with the election."
To show how sincere the government were in their desire to appoint proper officers I would refer to inspector G. H. Barbour of Charlottetown. This man, a provincial prohibition officer, was appointed without salary on April 23, 1923, and during his short tenure of office he had more seizures to his credit than all the other men on the whole island. That is to say, he had made six seizures within the space of six months. But because he
was too efficient he was dismissed on December 15, 1923, for which dismissal no reasons have so far been advanced.
There is in the waters of the gulf of St. Lawrence to-day a motor boat known as the Bernice which is costing the department $664 per month. That boat is supposed to be engaged in the work of surveying the shore. And who are on board her? One man on board has been for years rum-running to St. Pierre-Miquelon, and he abandoned that enterprise only when he lost his schooners on the rocky shores of Cape Breton in a storm. Thereupon he proceeded to sell liquor contrary to law and shortly after the new government of Nova Scotia came into power, finding no doubt that it was a rather dangerous business to carry on, he transferred it to his son. He is now working on this motor boat which is, as I say, ostensibly engaged in survey work, and it is common talk in that section of the country that the motor boat conveys liquor from vessels beyond the three-mile limit to this man's son on shore for him to sell by the glass.
Can this government claim that they have made reasonable efforts to enforce the customs laws? Why, that vote of $350,000 last year was nothing more than political camouflage: some men had to be rewarded prior to the election and they got their reward.
I turn now to another phase of the subject. I was sorry indeed that the Minister of Customs should attempt, as he did yesterday afternoon, to excuse everybody else and take the whole blame upon himself. I do not think he is doing himself justice. I did intend to say that we regret personally having been obliged to take the present step, but I fear the hon. gentleman might give me the same reply he was good enough to make to the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) yesterday. And as I have no wish to crucify anyone I shall not express that regret. No, Mr. Speaker, the minister need not take the whole blame. The blame for the neglect of properly enforcing the customs laws of this Dominion must rest with the entire cabinet. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) was himself on the 22nd day of January, 1925, aware of the situation so far as it relates to liquor activities in the Maritime provinces. I have under my hand a copy of a letter addressed to him by the Social Service Council of Nova Scotia, which letter, by the way, is among the files produced by the department for the information of the inquiry. The Social Service Council of Nova Scotia represents all the churches of that province, and other organizations, as follows: Church of England

speechtext: Read them all.

subtopic: REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext:
I might quote the Maria A. Howes, which cleared from Halifax on October 5, 1925, with 17,300 cases of liquor for Lima, Peru. She was back two days later, and cleared again with 17,000 cases for the same destination. Then the schooner Catherine M. Moulton cleared from Halifax for Havana on August 11, 1925, with 6,607 cases anrl 4 kegs of liquor. Four days later she cleared again for the same destination with 6,507 cases and 104 kegs. Not even an airoplane could make the trip from Halifax to Havana and be back in four days. That must have been known to the Customs officers.
Now I come to the schooner Morso, with registry at Lunenburg, Nova Scotia, which left Halifax for St. Pierre, Miquelon on August 13 with 2,6S2 cases and 185 kegs of liquor. In two days she cleared Halifax again; she must have made the round trip of 1,000 miles in 48 hours, allowing no time for unloading and loading. Then she cleared for Guanaija with 300 kegs of liquor in addition to her first shipment. Where did she get the liquor? Through the 260 odd vessels which cleared Halifax and St. John in 1925 you have the whole story.
Before I leave the question of liquor smuggling in Nova Scotia and the Maritime provinces generally I wish to say that there is conclusive evidence on file that these vessels never reached Nassau, Havana, the Azores, Lima, Peru, Porto Coles, Venezuela or Nicaragua, to which places they cleared. They inevitably found sale for their goods on the shores of the Maritimes or in "rum row" off the United States coast. I want to emphasize the point, Mr. Speaker, that no excise, customs or sales tax was paid on over 5,750,600 gallons of liquor shipped in the course of three years from these two Canadian ports and there are, at least, seven other ports in Canada where this is practised.
I asked a moment ago why the present Minister of Customs assumed all the responsibility in connection with the administration of customs laws; there is such a thing as adopting an heroic attitude at an uncalled for time. Members of the government were aware of the fact that smuggling of liquor had been going on. Members of this House will remember that in the spring of 1925 there was a coal strike in Cape Breton, and that in response to a plea for help the militia were sent to Glace Bay. In June, 1925, a seizure of liquor was made in the quarters of the Royal Canadian Dragoons at Glace Bay. That liquor was transported there in two motor cars from the motor boat Kiora, which boat had landed the liquor from a vessel outside the three mile limit. The House may ask ;f a prosecution was made then, and my answer is no. Why? Because the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald) intervened and said, "You cannot prosecute these men."

If my hon. friend has anything to say about August of that year he
can say it.

subtopic: REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext: I am asking you.

subtopic: REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext:
I expect the hon. member
to ask a sensible question. This liquor was unloaded from the vessel operating in "rum row"; landed by one of the fastest motor boats in that district and transported to the barracks, and neither the owners of the motor boat, the motor cars or the officers connected with the landing of that liquor were prosecuted, be* cause a minister of the crown, a member of this present government, intervened and prevented prosecution.
I come now, Mr. Speaker, to a motor boat known as the Cozy, of 10 tons, not registered. She left St. Pierre, Miquelon, on July 22, 1925, with 250 cases of whiskey; she arrived at Main-a-dieu, Cape Breton, on the morning of the 25th with nothing on board. There was no report inward and no report outward; she remained in Main-a-dieu until July 30, and was seized in Halifax on August 5, the date to which my hon. friend was referring. She was seized for having unloaded liquor on the shores of Cape Breton without making a report inward or outward. One of the friends of the government in Halifax wired the department and the present Minister of Customs .pleased the boat, or authorized a refund of the fine which had been paid on August 28th, and the fine was thereupon returned.
lNow I come to the schooner Rising Sun, wmch left Canso on September 23, 1925, with

Customs Inquiry-Mr. Doucet
a clearance for Nassau. I hope hon. mem. bers know the direction which would be taken in going from Canso to Nassau, but this schooner was in Charlottetown on September 26 and cleared again from Charlottetown for Nasau with 770 cases of liquor. She was hovering around the shores of the Northumberland strait, making no report to the customs and arrived at the out port of Canso on October 1 in ballast, empty. This schooner was seized and one of the sailors made an affidavit confirming every suspicion of the officers in that territory, but would you be surprised to learn that while the officers of the preventive service were making a close scrutiny of the district to get additional evidence the hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) wired the department to release the vessel, and she was released before the officers of the department working on the ground had a chance to report to their chief.
Now, Mr. Speaker, during the whole of the inquiry when we discussed this question *f ocean going vessels the question of territorial waters was always to the fore. That was brought about because for at least thirty-five years to the knowledge of the officers of the department who testified at that inquiry, what is known as the strait of Northumberland, the Baie des Chaleurs, and the gulf of St. Lawrence, inside of Cabot strait, were known to be Canadian waters and recognized as such, and every seizure made inside Cabot strait was recognized by the department who were sustained in that position by the courts in every case of appeal. In the month of June, 1923, we find that the schooner W. C. Kennedy, owned by the W. C. Kennedy Company of Lunenburg-which by the way was not known by the postmaster of Lunenburg when a registered letter was sent there by the department after the seizure, but whose secretary, apparently, is one Mr. Adams, who is also secretary for the Lunenburg Outfitting Company-left St. Pierre et Miquelon with 994 cases of liquor. She reached Halifax and remained there ten days waiting for orders. She cleared from Halifax on June 18, 1923, and took a clearance for Nassau in the Bahamas. She was next reported in the strait of Northumberland, seven miles off Pictou island, on June 26. That, as hon. gentlemen know, is in the opposite direction to the course for Nassau. The vessel was seized by the customs cruiser Margaret, and before the master had a chance to communicate with his fellows on shore, he replied to questions by Captain Alfred Lacouvee, of the Margaret. He stated it was true that he had a clearance for Nassau, but 'he had been told by the supercargo to lie off Pictou

and there take orders from the supercargo who had gone by land to make the necessary arrangements for the landing of the cargo. He further testified that when the seizure took place he had only 806 cases of liquor on board. He said that after leaving Halifax he had unloaded 188 cases of liquor in open motorboats outside of the three-mile limit on the Dartmouth shore. The schooner was seized, the cargo transferred to the steamer Margaret, and taken to Quebec. But, Sir, the hon member for the eonstitutency of Lunenburg, (Mr. Duff), realized that there was a possibility that by invoking the territorial water question he might have his schooner released.

subtopic: REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext: His schooner.

subtopic: REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext:
I said "his schooner," because if you look at Lloyd's register you will see that the W. C. Kennedy was registered in the hon. gentleman's name. Furthermore the captain of the vessel said that he was hired and his wages were paid by the hon member; but he had to take orders from the supercargo. Now the cargo was valued at $35,000 and the vessel at $20,000, and it was in the hands of the customs officers. The question may be asked now: What steps were taken to secure that seizure in the interests of the department? The answer is no steps whatsoever. The master of the schooner made three different affidavits to suit the needs of the occasion. These three affidavits, varying with each other in quite a degree, are to be found on the file. Counsel for the owners of the cargo and the schooner made a claim that the strait of Northumberland were not territorial waters, consequently the department would not hold the seizure and did not think of getting the opinion of the Department of Justice. Furthermore although the Department of Marine and Fisheries maintained that under the treaties that had been entered into those waters were considered as Canadian waters, they submitted to the claim advanced by counsel for the defendant without asking for an opinion from the Department of Justice. They ignored the affidavit made by the master of the ship before he had been in touch with his fellows on shore; they ignored the report made by the captain of their own cruiser; they released the vessel on the payment of $400; they returned the cargo of liquor which had been sent to Quebec back to Halifax to be loaded on another rum-running schooner going out of Halifax; and they refunded the sum of $400 which had been -made as a deposit in the first instance. I understand the Minister of Marine and Fisheries is to speak in this debate, and I want him to answer this

Customs Inquiry-Mr. Doucet
question for the benefit of myself and my constituents: if the waters of the strait of Northumberland are considered territorial waters for the purpose of deep sea fishing, how can they be anything else but Canadian waters for the purpose of preventing the smuggling of goods into Canada? The men whom I represent in this House claim, and rightly so, that if the waters of the strait of Northumberland, outside of the three-mile limit, are to be considered as international waters for the rum-running schooners of the Lunenburg crowd they can also be considered international waters in the interests of the lobster fishermen.
Now I come to the motorboat Jeanne d'Arc. This was an open boat 40 feet long and unregistered. She left St. Pierre et Miquelon and took a clearance for Nassau in the Bahamas, a distance of at least 2.000 miles, in the fall of 1923. On September 19 she was seized within three miles of the shores of Prince Edward Island. Her cargo of contraband liquors was transferred to the schooner Margaret, taken to the port of Quebec, and placed in the custom house there. On December 17, 1923, a telegram was sent by the department to put the Je.anne d'Arc in winter quarters. A copy of that telegram is on the file. On December 19 an additional telegram was sent arranging for a release and not to proceed with the order of placing the vessel in winter quarters. There is absolutely nothing on the files to show why the department changed its mind between December 17 and December 19. There is a memorandum on the file stating that a letter from the Hon. A. B. Copp for the Minister of Customs and Excise was attached, but that letter is not to be found on the file. At that time there was a by-election on in the county of Kent, the boat being owned in Buctouc'ne. The owners of that boat, who ordinarily are very active partisans, refrained from taking part in the election. There were two members of the government in that county and a gentleman who became a minister of the crown later on. Shortly after these men had made a pilgrimage throughout the country, the owners of the boat Jeanne d'Arc became enthusiastic supporters of the government, and the question is how could they change their minds overnight? The telegram of the 19th December shows the reason why. The vessel and the cargo being released, some excuse must be found. What excuse did they invoke to release the vessel three miles from the shore? They asked the captain of the cruiser a question, and they found the vessel was 5,770 yards from shore. If they had used a nautical mile in their calculations, it would
have meant more than 6,000 yards. But someone acquainted with mathematical problems in the department used the land mile and they found that 5,770 yards would be sufficient to get her outside the three land mile limit. Just as though you would proceed to measure molasses by a yardstick instead of measuring by the gallon measure, they used the land mile instead of the nautical mile; on that basis they found she was outside the three-mile limit, and they released the vessel. The question now is, how is it that they do not enforce the customs laws of this country?
I believe I have discussed at sufficient length the activities of the liquor fleet of Nova Scotia and the Maritime provinces, aided by the government in every respect. They granted clearances for the foreign ports when they knew the boat would never reach there. They granted a clearance to a port in South America where the trip would take about four months, but the boat was back in forty-eight hours and the liquor was landed on Canadian shores by motor boats. The ministers of the crown intervened and no prosecution resulted. The people of the Social Service Council of Canada asked the Prime Minister and the government to provide swift running motor boats for the purpose of watching the bays and inlets of Nova Scotia, and when the boat called the Rambler was seized in the fall of 1924, the speediest motor boat to be found on that shore, the preventive service wanted to get it for its own service. But because one rum-runner of Sydney wanted the boat for his own purposes in rum-running, and because his request was supported by the chief Liberal whip at that time, Mr. Kyte, representing Richmond, Cape Breton, the minister, in the month of January, 1926, said, "We can not handle the Rambler; sell it at once to the man in Sydney; make a sale without any loss of time."
The hon. member for Vancouver North this afternoon cited a number of cases. He failed to cite or forgot to cite the case of the famous Denise Larde case in which a seizure took place in the port of Quebec, but the goods were subsequently released without penalty, by the Department on a payment of $1,500, when the duty and sales tax amounted to $2,567.29. Why my hon. friend never referred to it, I know not. Is it because the man who was instrumental in bringing this revenue into the treasury was subsequently dismissed? And was it because he had arrested this party that an order issued from Ottawa a few days later that no arrests were to be made before reporting the cases to Ottawa?

Customs Inquiry-Mr. Doucet
I ask you, Sir, how can smuggling be prevented in this Dominion? When you find a notorious smuggler you cannot hold him, you cannot arrest him, you cannot stop him from going on his way until such time as you telephone to Ottawa or send a letter and wait three days for a reply. The facts brought out in the inquiry have shown conclusively to the public that there has been a lack of supervision in safeguarding the interests of this Dominion and the public treasury. The fact that all this violation of the law was known to every member of the cabinet, that this was going on aided and abetted and helped in some instances by members of the government, is shown conclusively by the evidence given in that inquiry. When appeals were made by responsible and even by distinguished persons of this Dominion asking fcr relief, the appeals fell on deaf ears. The Social Service Council of Nova Scotia asked the Department of Customs, and on the 22nd January, 192,5, asked the Prime Minister of this Dominion, to remedy the situation which had such a demoralizing effect on that section of the country, which was ruining the population, and was making it impossible to enforce the prohibition laws of the provinces in question, with the result that the public revenues were being cheated out of millions of dollars annually. That, Sir, was eighteen months ago, and were it not for the inquiry proposed as a result of the charges made in this house by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) on the 2nd of February last, no steps would yet have been taken by the department to clean up this state of affairs.
In the month of September a distinguished member of the clergy of the diocese cf Gaspe wrote to the Minister of Justice complaining of the illegal importation of liquor into that section of the province. The minister referred that letter to the Acting Minister of Customs and Excise, but with what effect I do not know because the same conditions continued.
I have throughout this debate endeavoured not to resort to cases such as those referred to by the hon. member for Vancouver North He would refuse to vote to bring names up in this House and then he would refer to those names after refusing to vote for the motion. He violated a gentleman's agreement with members of the committee not to expose certain information mentioned in the Duncan report. In the evidence and exhibits certain matters were referred to which had nothing to do with the customs and members of the committee decided, and I believe wisely and well, not to make them public. The hon. member, however, violated a gentleman's

agreement in bringing that matter belore the House and challenging the hon. member for Vancouver Centre to say why the Hon. Jacques Bureau had not been brought before the. inquiry. Did I wish to resort to citing case after case, I could do so I submit to the intelligence of members of the House that the case of the hon. member for North Sim-coe (Mr. Boys) is on a par with that of the hon. member for Charlevoix-Sagueaay (Mr. Casgrain), chief whip of the Litieral party, who appeared before the department on behalf of the owner of the barge Tremblay.
