speechtext:
Would the hon. gentleman repeat that statement? I did not catch it?
Mr. DOL'CET: The hon. member appeared before the department in defence of his client. He wanted a minimum fine imposed upon the owner of the barge Tremblay. He appeared not as a member of parliament, I believe, but as a professional man. and in the same way as a lawyer the hon. member for North Simcoe also appeared before the department to have his client's case settled. No favours were granted to the hon. member for North Simcoe because his .client paid double duty and sales tax, and he stated he did. But if you read the evidence you will find that the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay received consideration, because the man who was guilty of violating the customs laws of the Dominion, whose vessel valued at that time at $20,000 had been seized by the authorities, who was making $5,000 by transporting contraband goods from St. Pocras in the lower St. Lawrence to Montreal, paid the sum of $1,700 and placed $3,300 clear money in his pocket on the one trip.
When responsible people of this Dominion, when members of the Social Service Council of Nova Scotia, representing every church and fraternal organization of that province, when prominent clergymen of the lower St, Lawrence appeal to this government for redress against that army of liquor smugglers who are invading our shores, demoralizing our population, and striking consternation into the hearts of the people, I believe there is sufficient political honour and decency on the part of members of this parliament to rise and say: A stop must be put to this. Why, Sir, if this motion is lost on the division you will be penalizing the smaller fry, the men getting the lower salaries, and the men higher up will go scot-free. The complaint that is being made throughout the country to-day that the man higher up, holding a title of some kind or away up in society, can do

Customs Inquiry-Mr. Denis (Joliette)
anything he likes and get oS scot-free wnile the man who steals a loaf of bread goes to jail, will be true. If those who were debauched, if those who failed in their duty because the department was wrongly administered with the knowledge and connivance of ministers of this government are to be penalized to the extent of losing their positions and their pension money, I say that this government deserves the condemnation of this House because, with the knowledge of the facts in their possession, they should have months ago, aye, years ago, taken precautionary measures so that these things could not happen in this fair land of ours.

subtopic: REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
since this debate has originated, we have heard a number of speeches delivered that are really political speeches. The hon. member for Kent (Mr. Doucet) has delivered a political speech and I do not intend to follow him along that line. The times are momentous enough, the people of this country are eager enough in the administration of public affairs to warrant hon. members in pausing for one moment, forgetting political speeches, and addressing themselves to the reason, intelligence and integrity of their fellow-members as well as to the country at large.
The question now before parliament is not one of small importance; it is a most important issue because without doubt on the decision that will be rendered on the issue now before parliament serious consequences must arise. May I be permitted in opening my remarks to examine the amendment moved by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) ? His amendment is in part at least in direct contradiction of the speech which he made in this House yesterday. Speaking on June 22, at page 4819 of Hansard, the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) said:
With the report I am in accord, with one reservation, namely, the failure of the committee ito report a finding on the evidence referring to the conduct of the ministry,
This amendment goes very much further, containing as it does reproaches which are not voiced in the speech itself of the hon. gentleman. For the sake of brevity I shall refrain from analyzing these reproaches and shall confine myself instead to the general issue and try to demonstrate to the House that the case at present before parliament is not that which hon. gentlemen opposite have seen fit to argue. There are two aspects to this case, the political and the administrative, and hon. gentlemen opposite have devoted their entire attention to the former. Hardly
any practical suggestions have they vouchsafed from the administrative standpoint. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that this is too important an issue to be made a political football on either side of the House. In the course of my few remarks to-night I shall endeavour as best I can to show that if abuses have occurred the responsibility rests not with the present Minister of Customs (Mr. Boivin), nor with the minister who acted in the department, nor even with the ex-minister. Rather the trouble lies with the very system itself and the conditions which have grown up of late years under that system.
Hon. gentlemen opposite have been arguing for hours to establish the fact that smuggling has been going on in Canada on a large scale. To this no one takes exception; we all know perfectly well that of late years there has been a good deal of smuggling in this country. But I submit that in all countries where there is a tariff smuggling follows as a natural consequence. In the United States, during the past few years particularly, millions and tens of millions of dollars have been spent to prevent smuggling and in spite of these precautions enormous quantities of liquor have been smuggled into that country. In Canada also there has always been smuggling to a large extent. True, smuggling during the last few years may have increased, but I respectfully suggest that if it has increased the fault is not with any minister of customs either past or present. As we all know, in 1917-I think it was in that year-the government of the United States by the eighteenth amendment brought prohibition into force, and this law has been in existence in that country since that time. And ever since that amendment to the constitution of the United States that country has expended tens of millions of dollars to prevent liquor coming within its borders. Yet liquor has gone there in enormous quantities. Is not this enough to prove that it is by no means an easy task to prevent smuggling? Does it not show that not only has smuggling occurred in the past, as it is occuring to-day, but that it will prevail in the future as well? It is true that it is the duty of the minister to do his best to prevent it; towards this end he must adopt the best possible means at his disposal. But let us examine, before we condemn him, just what means he has at his disposal.
The report declares that there has been degeneracy in efficiency. That seems to be true, but if there is degeneracy in efficiency does the responsibility rest with the minister or with the system? I submit that it is a
4912	COMMONS
Customs Inquiry-Mr. Denis (Joliette)
consequence of new conditions which have arisen since 1918. I go further: I say that whether the minister be active or inactive, efficient or inefficient, such action as he may take does not amount to more than 5 per cent of the whole force that should be brought to bear upon the operations of smugglers. Now, what are the conditions? Until 1918, as we know, we had in Canada a Civil Service Act in relation to what is known as the inside service, and that service alone. In other words, the Civil Service Commission could appoint civil servants in the city of Ottawa, but outside of that, in Toronto, Montreal, Vancouver, and in all ports where customs revenues are collected, the Minister of Customs had the right and the duty to select his employees in the various offices. If, therefore, the employees were inefficient the fault was the minister's; he having chosen them, he alone was responsible. By the Civil Service Act of 1918, however, this condition was changed. Now it is not my purpose at the moment to discuss the merits or the demerits of the Civil Service Act; I do not propose to argue the question whether that act ought or ought not to have been passed. The merits of the act, generally speaking, I leave aside. I contend, however, that mistakes so flagrant might never have been made had the appointment of detectives been left outside the scope of the Civil Service Commission. The Customs department comprises two distinct branches, one of administration and the other the preventive service. But even in the administrative branch officials may be dishonest; even in that branch they may be bought. So that if dishonest officials are bought, the minister cannot be held responsible inasmuch as they are not his appointees. They are the appointees of the Civil Service Commission.
Now, Sir, think of it, an institution that collects something like two or three hundred million dollars a year whose minister has not the privilege of appointing its employees. The most important of our chartered banks is the Bank of Montreal. What would you think, Sir, if to-morrow the president should be told that henceforth all the employees of the institution would be chosen by a board independent of his board of directors-the Civil Service Commission? Do you think for one moment that the bank could carry on satisfactorily under such circumstances?

subtopic: REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext:
Is it not a fact that
even in a corporation like the Bank of Montreal only certain of its officials have the right 
to choose the employees, as in this case the Civil Service Commission has the right to choose employees for the government? Is there very much differnce?

subtopic: REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext: In the case of the Bank of Montreal the high officials-the president, the board of directors and the managers-choose the employees, and those high officials are directly responsible to the shareholders. In a word, they are part of the organization of the bank. But in this case the Civil Service Commission is not a part of the government, it is not a part of any department in the government, but is altogether independent of it.

subtopic: REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext:
Surely my hon. friend
would not state that the Civil Service Commission is not a part of the government? It was created by the government for that specific purpose.

subtopic: REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext: The Civil Service Commission is not a part of the government inasmuch as it is absolutely independent of the government; while the directors of the Bank of Montreal are under the direct control of the shareholders and can be replaced by the shareholders at the annual general meeting. The directors of the bank are directly responsible to its shareholders; the Civil Service Commission is responsible to no one. What I have said of the Bank of Montreal will apply as well to the Canadian Pacific railway. Surely anyone who would propose to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company that their employees should be chosen by a commission would be treated with contempt. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company's employees are. responsible to their superiors, and those superiors in turn are responsible to the board of directors, which in turn is responsible to the shareholders; in short, it is one organization.

subtopic: REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext:
Might I ask the hon.
gentleman if in this case the employees of the government service are not responsible to the government? The minister of each department has the right to dispense with any employees whose services are not satisfactory.

subtopic: REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext:
I do not agree
with my hon. friend. Technically the minister has the right, but in practice he cannot dispense with the services of any employee without cause or without reason.

subtopic: REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext:
Why should he desire
to dispense with the services of any employee without cause or without reason?

Customs Inquiry-Mr. Denis (Joliette)

subtopic: REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext:
My hon. friend's objection only makes my case so much stronger. This is my answer to him. During the course of the inquiry of the Customs committee, extending over four or five months, certain officials have been found delinquent in the discharge of their duty and it is recommended that their services be dispensed with. Now I ask my hon. friend,- does he not think in view of the wholesale smuggling that has been going on for several yeears that there are not many other officials equally blameworthy, but whose delinquencies could not be brought home to them by the committee within the time at their disposal? Undoubtedly-and unfortunately-there are. If it took four months for the committee to discover six delinquent officers, how can the minister, without continuing the investigation, bring to book those other guilty men? It is impossible. Very seldom indeed are departmental officials found guilty of wrongdoing, and it is only when this is amply proved that the minister dispenses with their services. The minister is not independent of his officials, and as long as that unsatisfactory condition continues you cannot expect his department to be thoroughly efficient. I go further; not only so, but you cannot hold him responsible for that inefficiency without doing him grave injustice. This is only by way of illustration in matters of administration.
But more is involved in this case. The preventive service is also under the control of the Civil Service Commission. It is recommended in the report that the preventive service should be reorganized and
10 p.m. strengthened, that in reality it should become a detective agency. Now, imagine a detective agency having to go to an independent body-the Civil Service Commission-for its men. Think of the Pinkerton detective agency, the Field detective agency, Scotland Yard or La Surete, having to resort to an independent body to provide them with detectives. Could anything be more ridiculous?

subtopic: REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext:
Was that part of the
service appointed directly by the minister under the patronage system as efficient as that appointed by the Civil Service Commission?

subtopic: REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext: We can only judge of the efficacy of any measure from the results obtained, and we know that since the system was changed in 1918 the department has been steadily degenerating.

subtopic: REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext: Who is responsible?

subtopic: REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext: It is all very well to blame the minister. The minister may have had something to do with it-I will come to that in a moment-but I contend that one of the main reasons why this service has been degenerating is that we declared in the Civil Service Act that an organization of detectives must go to a foreign body for their recruits. That is absolutely impracticable and, I submit, absurd. Therefore the first reason why there has been degeneration and inefficiency is the fact that these men are chosen by the Civil Service Commission; they are independent of the minister and he cannot control them. Had the minister control of these men I would say he was responsible for them, but when he has no control he cannot have responsibility.

subtopic: REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman allow a question?

subtopic: REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext: With pleasure.

subtopic: REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext: Is it not a fact that any of these officials may be dismissed without consulting the Civil Service Commission?

subtopic: REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext: Yes. The minister can dismiss but he cannot appoint, so what is the use of dismissing a man if you cannot appoint another whom you choose in his place?

subtopic: REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext: Every time he gets an inefficient official he can be dismissed.

subtopic: REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext: Yes, he has the right to dismiss him but it is well known that the civil service is pretty well filled up in some quarters with inefficient men. I am not attacking anyone when I say this; we know that they remain where they are because the ministers dare not dismiss them. They are in the service to stay and they stay.

subtopic: REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext: Allow me another question. Is it not a fact, as was stated by the hon. member who spoke just before the hon. gentleman who now has the floor, that the officers found most inefficient in this investigation were those who had been appointed not by the Civil Service Commission but by the department?

subtopic: REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext:
No official has been appointed by the department. Who was so appointed; was it Bisaillon? Bisaillon was appointed by the Civil Service Commission like the rest. I would like my hon. friend to name one official who was appointed by the department. I do not say this for the sake of discussion, but we must
4914	COMMONS
Customs Inquiry-Mr. Denis (Joliette)
be plain about these things. Not one official in that department is appointed other than by the Civil Service Commission, and not one promotion can be made except through the Civil Service Commission.

subtopic: REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext: Then I ask the hon. member whether or not the statement is true that the most inefficient officials were those appointed before the Civil Service Commission had control of the outside service?

subtopic: REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext: Does my hon. friend mean before 1918, when the Civil Service Act was passed?

subtopic: REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext: Take the case of the Bank of Montreal. Surely that institution can dismiss an official when found to be dishonest. Is there any difference in the two cases?

subtopic: REPORT OP SPECIAL COMMITTEE-MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE AND AMENDMENTS THERETO

My hon. friends opposite say that it is a charge which should disqualify him and for which he should be censured by the House. If hon. members would divest themselves for one instant of all political tendencies, all political affiliations, and consider this matter clearly and reasonably, I believe very few of them would come to the conclusion that for this particular action the Minister of Customs should be so judged. A man is not to be judged for a single action in his life. If that were so I know that a few members of this

Customs Inquiry-Mr. Lucas
House would possibly regret some of their past actions. But I do not look at things in that way. It is human and only fair to judge a man by his conduct as a whole and not by any one particular act which, though regarded as reprehensible by some, may be considered in a different light by others. I would rather take the conduct of the Minister of Customs as a whole and judge him on the sum total of his achievements, his activities, and his talents. Let me remind hon. gentlemen that the reputation of a public man is precious, and before it is impugned we ought to weigh the circumstances very carefully. This country has need on both sides of politics of men of the class of the Hon. George H. Boivin. The Minister of Customs has shown in this House a character, an ability and an intelligence second to those of no other hon. member. He is a man of courage, a man of energy; and I believe that in the interests of Canada, in the interests of the department itself, he should remain Minister of Customs. If that department is to be saved no man is better able than he, with his youth, his courage, and his activity, to restore it to the position it should have held long ago.
It is the duty of members of - parliament, representing the Canadian people, always to help and encourage and to promote the request of the people for our public men. The responsibilities of public life are not so easy. It is not so easy to spend months in the city of Ottawa, beautiful though it be, to the exclusion of one's personal affairs. And after the Minister of Customs has devoted his energies to the service of his country in work involving sacrifice, is he now to be cited before this House on mere piffle, a matter of insignificance? Are we to condemn him, forgetting the services he has rendered, simply because he is alleged to have done something which although represensible in the opinion of others is not so, in my opinion at any rate?
Numerous recommendations are made in the report, and what in my view is of prime importance is that the Minister of Customs, and he alone, should be responsible for the officials of his department. I am not asking that the Civil Service Act be done away with, but I do say that it should be amended to give the minister the opportunity of choosing his own personnel, so far at least as the preventive service is concerned. Indeed, I would include the officials of the department; I do not refer to ordinary clerks, but to all officials of responsibility. I would allow the minister to make his own appointments and if, then, these officials did not perform their 14011-312
duties satisfactorily, the minister would be responsible to parliament. The minister should also have the right to control his department and its employees. I would suggest that a permanent committee of the House be appointed in relation to customs affairs. We have a Public Accounts committee ; why not have a committee on customs so -that the department might from session to session be subject to investigation? If such a committee existed those who had charges to make against the department might lay them before that committee instead of waiting for years, as has happened in this case, before bringing up the matter. With the minister solely responsible for the personnel of his department, and with a free hand to manage the affairs of the department as he saw fit, if he. failed to discharge his office efficiently, whoever the minister might be, then he should be censured by parliament. But only under such circumstances would the minister be fully responsible for the acts of his officials and be in consequence subject to such criticism as is proposed in this amendment.
Whatever the decision may be, I hope that hon. gentlemen will very seriously review the excellent work of the Minister of Customs before returning the verdict sought by the amendment.

speechtext:
As we
shall shortly be called upon to decide upon the question before the House, and as I shall be required to register what will be the most important vote in my whole parliamentary career, I feel it my duty to state my view of the situation. I want to make it clear at the outset that however I may vote, or whatever remarks I may make, on this occasion, I am moved by no spirit of personal antagonism to any member of the government. During the last four years and in the course of the present session, in any business I have had to transact with members of the cabinet, I have always been treated with the utmost courtesy and consideration. But I should be untrue to the trust reposed in me if I were to let personal friendships come between me and the duty which I feel I owe to the people whom I represent. I was bom and brought up in the good old province of Ontario and one of the things I was taught from my youth was to look up to our parliamentary institutions, the highest representative bodies, of our country.
The question before the House to night is one that transcends personalities or parties. It is a question that strikes at the very fundamentals of our public life. It is therefore



Customs Inquiry-Mr. Lucas
incumbent upon every hon. member to subordinate party considerations to public duty and as a true Canadian to cut out this cancer which is gnawing at the heart of our body politic. I am not going to condemn in any way the hon. Minister of Customs (Mr. Boivin). He is a man of outstanding ability, but in my opinion the greater his ability the greater his sin. But, Mr. Speaker, not only is one minister involved; censure falls equally on every member of the government. When you read the evidence-and I have followed it very closely throughout the sittings of the committee-and on pages 120 to 132 you peruse the correspondence between the Commercial Protective Association and the Prime Minister, it seems to me you can come to no other conclusion than that the Prime Minister at least was conversant with conditions in the Customs department. What strikes me more forcibly than anything else is the fact that the Prime Minister (|Mr. Mackenzie King), being conversant with those conditions, subsequently appointed to the Senate of Canada a man who is certainly not entitled to that high position. When I reflect that the Prime Minister toured this country during the last campaign and told the people how he was going to reform the Senate, and afterwards appointed a gentleman who had debauched the very life of Canada by encouraging bootlegging, with its slimy trail over the whole land, I am grievously disappointed, and nothing short of a censure of this government will satisfy the people of Canada on this point.
There are those who think that to-night the fate of the Liberal party is at stake. Mr. Speaker, I am not concerned with the fate of the Liberal party or of the Conservative party, but I am vitally concerned with the fate of the Progressive movement, a movement that many of our people are looking forward to as the one hope of cleaning up our public life and bringing about a better condition of affairs in this fair Canada of ours. I do not think there is an hon. member in this corner of the House that would be in his seat tonight but for that movement which we represent. When I think of those people back in Alberta from whom I come, who had got almost to the point of despair, feeling they could not trust to the party machine-picked candidates to carry out their pledges and their promises, and who said, "We must pick out men from among ourselves, and we will make sacrifices to pay their campaign expenses so they will not be bound to any political party," and when I recall the sacrifices that some of those men and women have made during the past few years to foster this movefMr. Lucas.]
ment, I would certainly 'be recreant to my trust if I did not stand up for the principles they sent me to maintain and uphold in parliament.
The Prime Minister stated in a recent debate that if the government should be defeated we would be faced with a general election. I want to say, Sir, that I feel I would be unworthy of my position as a member of this House if I allowed any threat of that kind to prevent me from doing my duty. I feel that I have been sent here for a certain purpose, and I intend to try to carry out that purpose. If a general election should come and I go down in the fight, then I shall feel proud that I have gone down fighting for the principles which I was sent here to uphold. I appeal to every member in this corner of the House, to every member of this Progressive party, to stand up to-night for those principles which they have been sent to this House to uphold. I would appeal particularly to the only lady member of this House. All the people of Canada are watching what will take place when the vote is registered. When I think of the misery and suffering which this bootlegging traffic has caused the women and children throughout Canada, I am proud that we have one woman representative, and I feel sure that she will deal justly with their cause. Sir George Etienne Cartier once said: If all the women could be banded together simply and solely for the good of humanity, they would exert an influence such as has never been felt before.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I could have dealt with a number of the cases which have been disclosed in the evidence, but I feel that as they have already been placed before the House anything further on my part would be simply superfluous. I want to say again, Sir, that I feel this is the most important vote that has come before this House this session, and I trust every member will do his duty.
Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg
North Centre): Mr. Speaker, there are occasions on which I presume most, of us would prefer not to have the responsibilities of membership in this House, and undoubtedly this is such an occasion. The more I study this question the more complicated it becomes, and yet as we are all called upon to cast a vote one way or the other, and we cannot very well shirk that vote, it seems to me it is not right to give a silent vote, but rather as far as possible to set before the House and the country the considerations which move one in coming to a decision on an important question of this character.

I would call the attention of hoD. members to the fact that this House pf Commons, which is primarily a legislative body, is these days turned into a court; but I would add that under existing circumstances impartial justice seems to me to be impossible in this court. Let us look at the situation. AVe have prosecutors and defendants, and these also are the jury and the judge, for if we really look at this situation frankly we must acknowledge that one party is very largely playing the role of prosecutor to-night, and has been for the last few days, while to a very considerable extent the other party is playing the role of defendant, and yet we are all called upon to act as jury in this case and even as judge. Now, there is not much doubt that in a case of this character hon. members are influenced by partisan bias or partisan consideration. I made a similar statement a few days ago in connection with Peace River election case, and I think my hon. friend from St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr Cahan) then interjected, " No, no." And yet the vote which was subsequently taken absolutely corroborated my statement, because it was almost entirely along party lines. I cannot conceive that the judgment of the people would again and again in legal matters split along purely party lines. So 1ft us be frank and say that in a case of this character it is extremely difficult for the most honest and honourable men-and I take it that despite some cheap sneers hurled across the floor the large majority of this House are honest and honourable men-I say it is very difficult in such a case for us not to be biased by partisan considerations. We have here a most phenomenal situation. The last vote on a want of confidence motion was in connection with the Kennedy case and yet Mr. Kennedy was the key man, shall I say, in the special committee investigating this matter. We have this situation, that the man who is presumably the most impartial, or in a position to be the most impartial, member will be accused in his vote on such an occasion as this of either inclining towards the government or, as I heard someone who knows Mr. Kennedy put it, of leaning backward in order to be straight.

I think it is rather a dangerous practice that perhaps is growing on us, to claim that we and we only have such a policy and are true to our convictions and to our country. Mr. Speaker, I rise only to a point of order again. I contend that this is not an amendment to the amendment. The same relativity which must obtain between an amendment and a motion is not the relativity which must obtain .between an amendment to an amendment and the amendment. An amendment to an amendment must deal with nothing but the subject matter of the amendment. An amendment to a motion

does not require necessarily to deal only with the subject matter of the motion. This is only too plainly a mere device for getting rid of any decision on the amendment. If this is brought before the House, the House might decide on the merits of it; but if it decided in its favour, that would prevent the House from .deciding on the merits of the amendment, which is something wholly different from this.
Although I have not had time to go into the rules thoroughly, the rule is that an amendment to an amendment must necessarily be an amendment to that amendment and not a different amendment. This is a different amendment altogether. This could be moved after the amendment is defeated, but it cannot be moved as an amendment to that amendment. The effect would be, as is indeed evidently the intention, to bring something in to which there is no special objection, get a vote upon it and thereby get rid of the amendment that is before the House. Against that course I protest and in that protest I believe I am supported by the best authorities. It is certainly unfair to have this matter decided adversely now in any case.
